articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Issues New General Licenses, and Amends FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions enforcement in these regions.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions programs.

Additionally, OFAC amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further clarity and guidance regarding the updated sanctions and general licenses. This move is intended to assist individuals and entities in complying with the evolving regulatory landscape.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target entities involved in the alleged theft of trade secrets, with China's Ministry of Commerce criticizing the move and warning of countermeasures.

In response to these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the PAIPA sanctions.

The U.S. action reflects a continued focus on protecting American intellectual property and addressing concerns related to economic espionage. China has urged the U.S. to lift the sanctions on five Chinese firms, stating that their rapid development in AI stems from independent innovation and open cooperation.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This amendment, GL 60A, replaces and supersedes GL 60, extending the authorization period for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.

The authorization period has been extended from its original end date of October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027. This extension aims to facilitate ongoing humanitarian aid and recovery efforts in the country.
Venezuela-related FAQ 1263 was also amended to reflect the extended authorization end date, providing updated guidance for those involved in earthquake relief activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities and a Cuban Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions are part of a broader U.S. effort targeting Iranian financial actors and alleged financial links between Cuba and Iran.

The Department of State sanctioned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank, for operating in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy and for allegedly providing services to Karafarin Bank, an Iranian financial institution sanctioned by the United States since 2020.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions. These include Russia-related GL 128D and GL 130B concerning certain activities involving Lukoil International GmbH (LIG) and related entities, extending authorizations until April 24, 2027.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Politician Jorge Rodriguez from Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list on October 14, 2026.

Rodriguez, who serves as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, was initially designated in 2018. This delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons attempting to deal with him.
This action comes amid Washington's latest push for diplomacy and expansion of energy investment in Venezuela, signaling a potential shift in U.S. policy towards the country.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Al Jazeera / Steptoe

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security.

Specifically, OFAC designated four individuals and 11 entities allegedly linked to Cartel del Noreste (CDN), a Mexico-based cartel. This action is OFAC's largest sanctions action to date targeting CDN, imposed pursuant to E.O. 14059, which targets the international proliferation of illicit drugs.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global illicit drug trade and combating terrorism financing networks.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of various sanctions programs.
Bank of America agreed to pay $11,662,930 for 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This settlement is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for deficiencies in the bank's anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, ICC Designation, and Burma Delisting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

In a separate action, OFAC announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This designation reflects ongoing U.S. policy regarding the ICC.

Additionally, OFAC announced a Burma-related designation removal, indicating a change in the sanctions posture concerning certain entities or individuals previously targeted under the Burma sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license, GL 135, authorizes certain transactions related to imports of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. until April 7, 2027.

This action follows President Trump's executive order on October 16, 2026, which waived the majority of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

The issuance of this General License and the broader waivers indicate a complex and evolving U.S. approach to sanctions against Russia, balancing punitive measures with certain economic considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These designations are part of ongoing efforts to target entities and individuals supporting the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions. This aims to balance sanctions pressure with humanitarian or other policy considerations.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, further adjusting the scope of permissible activities under the Russia sanctions program. This reflects the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy in response to geopolitical developments.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: On October 12, 2026, the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, marking one of the most significant sanctions developments since 2022.

This package primarily focuses on listings, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, including 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals. The measures target companies forming the 'core' of Russia's military-industrial ecosystem, involved in producing components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

The EU's action responds to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine and recent attacks on civilian infrastructure, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Hill Dickinson / Clyde & Co

articles.headline: EU Sanctions North Korean and Russian Entities for Supporting DPRK Weapons Programs
body: On October 12, 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.
articles.source: Council of the EU / NK News

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11.6 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $11,662,930 against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. This penalty is part of a settlement agreement for apparent violations of various sanctions programs.
The violations involved 475 instances of apparent breaches of sanctions targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This substantial fine underscores the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs for financial institutions to prevent illicit transactions and adhere to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses U.S. of Threatening Countries Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures in an effort to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running embargo against the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated on October 21, 2026, that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington's ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz were personally leading this campaign, which he alleged had been ongoing for months.

The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in support of resolutions calling for an end to the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba almost every year since 1992, with the embargo itself in place for over six decades.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including Major Penalties for BSA Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting significant penalties and prohibition orders.

Among the actions, the OCC issued a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs), and customer due diligence violations.

Additionally, the OCC assessed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file SARs, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. Prohibition orders were also issued against Jennifer Hamblin and Christopher Organista for embezzling customer funds.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
